Tasmanian senator says it was ‘extremely difficult decision to make’ and he will leave ‘proud and grateful but exhausted’ Liberal frontbencher Jonno Duniam will quit politics before the end of the year, in another major blow to the struggling Coalition which is experiencing its lowest levels of popularity in decades. The Tasmanian senator, who has been in parliament since 2016, said it was an “extremely difficult decision to make” but one he had been considering for “quite some time” to spend more time with family. “I have spent the past 25 years in politics, the last 10 of those as a senator for Tasmania – and I have given everything to these responsibilities, often at the expense of family,” he said in a statement on Sunday.

Tasmanian Liberal senator Jonathon Duniam will quit politics before the next federal election, saying he wants to put his family ahead of his career. Duniam, the opposition’s home affairs and immigration spokesman, will retire before the end of this year after 25 years in politics, including 10 years in the Senate. “I have given everything to these responsibilities, often at the expense of family,” he said in a statement. “It is time I reversed my priorities and I can’t do that if I am to stay in politics.” The 43-year-old said his three sons had grown up for large chunks of their childhood without him around and he could no longer keep doing that. He said his family had paid the price of his absence and he wanted to spend less time flying away for work.

The home affairs minister, Tony Burke, told Sky News on Sunday Duniam was one of the opposition’s “best and brightest”. The 43-year-old acknowledged his announcement came at a difficult time for the Coalition, who, on current polling data, could be wiped out as the opposition at the next federal election if One Nation’s surge in popularity remains. In May, a Redbridge Group/Accent Research poll published in the Australian Financial Review showed One Nation’s primary vote had surpassed Labor and the Coalition for the first time. Earlier this week, Tony Pasin, a conservative Liberal from rural South Australia and a shadow minister, suggested his party and One Nation “work hand-in-glove to defeat Labor” by arranging a deal not to run in the same seats. The suggestion was quickly rejected by Taylor, and Liberal senator James Paterson criticised the suggestion as “premature”.

Liberal frontbencher Jonno Duniam will quit politics before the end of the year, in another major blow to the struggling Coalition which is experiencing its lowest levels of popularity in decades.

The Tasmanian senator, who has been in parliament since 2016, said it was an “extremely difficult decision to make” but one he had been considering for “quite some time” to spend more time with family.

“I leave federal politics proud and grateful but exhausted.”

Duniam, who serves as the shadow home affairs minister, said he had informed the opposition leader, Angus Taylor, who asked him to finish the Coalition’s immigration policy work.

Tasmanian Liberal senator Jonathon Duniam will quit politics before the next federal election, saying he wants to put his family ahead of his career.

Duniam, the opposition’s home affairs and immigration spokesman, will retire before the end of this year after 25 years in politics, including 10 years in the Senate.

“I have given everything to these responsibilities, often at the expense of family,” he said in a statement.

“It is time I reversed my priorities and I can’t do that if I am to stay in politics.”

The 43-year-old said his three sons had grown up for large chunks of their childhood without him around and he could no longer keep doing that.

He said his family had paid the price of his absence and he wanted to spend less time flying away for work.

Duniam said even before entering the Senate his roles had meant long hours and heavy travel and the decision to leave was an easy one.

“25 years is a long time in any vocation and, when you take your role seriously, it always comes first,” he said.

Duniam acknowledged he was leaving at a hard time for the federal Coalition but backed its direction.

He praised opposition leader Angus Taylor and Nationals senator Matt Canavan, saying “no two people” were better equipped to lead the country back to success.

The senator listed achievements including saving the Mersey hospital and securing $730m for its operation in 2017, backing forestry and aquaculture and fighting for the future of 5,000 salmon jobs.

He also pointed to protecting funding for emergency relief programs and leading multi-partisan campaigns to secure Tasmania’s share of GST.

Duniam said Taylor had asked him to stay on briefly to finish work on the Coalition’s immigration policies, including its Australian Values migration plan.

He described representing Tasmania as “a blessing and the honour of a lifetime” and said he was leaving behind cherished friendships built over more than a decade.

Duniam won his Senate seat in 2016 before defeating Abetz for the top spot on the ticket ahead of the 2022 election.

payload.title: Australian liberaalisenaattori Jonno Duniam jättää politiikan
payload.summary: Tasmanialainen liberaalisenaattori Jonno Duniam aikoo vetäytyä politiikasta ennen vuoden loppua. Päätös osuu vaikeaan hetkeen Australian oppositiokoalitiolle, jonka kannatus on paineessa.
payload.content:
Tasmanialainen liberaalisenaattori Jonno Duniam aikoo jättää politiikan ennen vuoden loppua ja asettaa perheensä uransa edelle. Opposition eturiviin kuuluva 43-vuotias Duniam on edustanut Tasmaniaa senaatissa vuodesta 2016, toiminut politiikassa yhteensä 25 vuotta ja kuvannut päätöstään erittäin vaikeaksi.

## Päätös perheen vuoksi

Duniam sanoi harkinneensa lähtöään jo pitkään. Hän kertoi lähtevänsä politiikasta ylpeänä ja kiitollisena, mutta väsyneenä. Lausunnossaan hän sanoi antaneensa tehtävilleen kaikkensa, usein perheensä kustannuksella.

Duniam on opposition sisäasioiden ja maahanmuuton tiedottaja. Hän on ollut senaattorina 10 vuotta, ja hänen mukaansa tehtävät ovat vaatineet jatkuvaa poissaoloa kotoa. Duniam sanoi, että hänen kolme poikaansa ovat kasvaneet suuren osan lapsuudestaan ilman hänen läsnäoloaan.

Hänen mukaansa perhe on maksanut hinnan hänen poissaolostaan. Duniam sanoi haluavansa nyt kääntää tärkeysjärjestyksensä, eikä se hänen mukaansa onnistu, jos hän jatkaa politiikassa. Hän kertoi myös haluavansa viettää vähemmän aikaa työmatkoilla.

## Lähtö vaikeaan aikaan oppositiolle

Duniamin ilmoitus on takaisku Australian liberaaleille ja laajemmalle oppositiokoalitiolle. Hän itse myönsi ilmoituksen tulevan vaikeaan aikaan koalitiolle, jonka kannatus on lähteiden mukaan historiallisen heikolla tasolla. Nykyisten mielipidemittausten perusteella koalition asema oppositiossa voisi heikentyä tuntuvasti seuraavissa liittovaltiovaaleissa, jos One Nation -puolueen nousu jatkuu.

Toukokuussa julkaistun Redbridge Groupin ja Accent Researchin mittauksen mukaan One Nationin ensisijainen kannatus nousi ensimmäistä kertaa sekä työväenpuolueen että koalition edelle. Samalla liberaalien sisällä on käyty keskustelua siitä, miten puolueen pitäisi suhtautua One Nationiin vaalistrategiassa.

## Puolueessa keskustellaan suunnasta

Etelä-Australiasta tuleva konservatiivinen liberaalipoliitikko ja varjoministeri Tony Pasin ehdotti aiemmin tällä viikolla, että liberaalit ja One Nation voisivat tehdä yhteistyötä työväenpuolueen voittamiseksi sopimalla, etteivät ne asettaisi ehdokkaita samoihin vaalipiireihin. Ehdotus torjuttiin nopeasti liberaalijohdossa, ja liberaalisenaattori James Paterson piti sitä ennenaikaisena.

Australian sisäministeri Tony Burke kuvasi Duniamia sunnuntaina Sky Newsille yhdeksi opposition kyvykkäimmistä poliitikoista. Duniamin lähtö lisää muutospainetta tilanteessa, jossa oppositio hakee suuntaa ennen seuraavia liittovaltiovaaleja.

Hän sanoo päätöksen johtuvan halusta asettaa perhe etusijalle.
Lähtö tapahtuu aikana, jolloin Australian oppositiokoalitio kamppailee kannatuspaineiden kanssa.

Tasmanian senator says it was ‘extremely difficult decision to make’ and he will leave ‘proud and grateful but exhausted’ Liberal frontbencher Jonno Duniam will quit politics before the end of the year, in another major blow to the struggling Coalition which is experiencing its lowest levels of popularity in decades. The Tasmanian senator, who has been in parliament since 2016, said it was an “extremely difficult decision to make” but one he had been considering for “quite some time” to spend more time with family. “I have spent the past 25 years in politics, the last 10 of those as a senator for Tasmania – and I have given everything to these responsibilities, often at the expense of family,” he said in a statement on Sunday.

Tasmanian Liberal senator Jonathon Duniam will quit politics before the next federal election, saying he wants to put his family ahead of his career. Duniam, the opposition’s home affairs and immigration spokesman, will retire before the end of this year after 25 years in politics, including 10 years in the Senate. “I have given everything to these responsibilities, often at the expense of family,” he said in a statement. “It is time I reversed my priorities and I can’t do that if I am to stay in politics.” The 43-year-old said his three sons had grown up for large chunks of their childhood without him around and he could no longer keep doing that. He said his family had paid the price of his absence and he wanted to spend less time flying away for work.

The home affairs minister, Tony Burke, told Sky News on Sunday Duniam was one of the opposition’s “best and brightest”. The 43-year-old acknowledged his announcement came at a difficult time for the Coalition, who, on current polling data, could be wiped out as the opposition at the next federal election if One Nation’s surge in popularity remains. In May, a Redbridge Group/Accent Research poll published in the Australian Financial Review showed One Nation’s primary vote had surpassed Labor and the Coalition for the first time. Earlier this week, Tony Pasin, a conservative Liberal from rural South Australia and a shadow minister, suggested his party and One Nation “work hand-in-glove to defeat Labor” by arranging a deal not to run in the same seats. The suggestion was quickly rejected by Taylor, and Liberal senator James Paterson criticised the suggestion as “premature”.
